newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Erste bares shareholder friendly merger.
newsitem.headline: Erste bares shareholder friendly merger.

text.p: Die Erste, announcing the terms of the merger with GiroCredit, said on Friday the exchange ratio for shareholders in the two represented a shareholder friendly transaction unparalleled in Austria.

"The terms of the exchange offer have been designed to ensure fair treatment for all shareholders, to simplify the capital structure and to give all preference shareholders the opportunity to participate in the ordinary equity of the merged bank," member of Die Erste's executive board Reinhard Ortner told a news conference.

Following the merger which will create Austria's second largest banking group with combined assets of around 670 billion schillings, Die Erste will account for 59 percent of the valuation of the new bank while GiroCredit will account for 41 percent.
This translates into an exchange ratio of five new shares in Die Erste for shares in GiroCredit, or 1:2.4. The exchange applies to both GiroCredit ordinary and preferred shares.
Die Erste preference shareholders can exchange their shares into the new Die Erste ordinary voting shares on a 1:1 basis.

Die Erste's holding company AVS will also make preference shareholders in both banks an alternative cash offer of 543 schillings per preference share in Die Erste and 305 schillings per preference share in GiroCredit.

Die Erste, also known as First Austrian, said it would offer approximately one third of the banks' consolidated capital for sale to Austrian and international institutional investors and retail investors in Austria through an initial public offering (IPO).
The IPO, scheduled at the latest for spring next year, is expected to be the largest Austrian share offer to date.
UBS, advisers to the company and global coordinator of the IPO, said the offering would be a landmark transaction for the Austrian Stock Exchange.
"It will be a highly liquid share and will become one of the major constituents of the ATX," a member of UBS' advising team told Reuters.

"The management decided to make this a very shareholder friendly transaction and to treat all classes of shareholders equally (by giving them the option to change their shares into ordinary voting shares)," he said.
The smoothly-executed merger of the two savings bank giants lies in stark contrast to the bitterly contested merger of market leader Bank Austria with Creditanstalt CABV_p.VI in January.
The privatisation of Creditanstalt was marred by political gerrymandering that threatened to bring down Austria's government coalition of dominant Social Democrats and conservative People's Party.
The conservatives had bitterly fought to keep conservative stronghold Creditanstalt out of the reach of Social-Democrat dominated Bank Austria.
"Die Erste and GiroCredit are apolitical," said one observer who declined to be named.
Trading in the preferred shares of both banks was suspended by the Vienna bourse on June 30. Trading will resume on July 7.
